source_text: De anima contra philosophos (ap. Joannem Damascenum, Sacra parallela) (fragmenta) ΠΕΡΙ ΨΥΧΗΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΩΝ 1 Ὁ Θεὸς τὰ πάντα πληροῖ ὑπ' οὐδενὸς περιοριζόμενος· ὁ γὰρ ὑπὸ τόπου μὴ περιοριζόμενος πάντως ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ (∆αυῒδ) ὑμνολογίαν ἔσται· εἰ γὰρ ἔξω λέγοιτο τόπου τινός, ἀνάγκη περιορίζεσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπ' ἐκείνου οὗπερ στερίσκεται· ὅλος οὖν ἐν πᾶσι γινόμενος, οὐδαμῶς ἐξ ἑτέρων εἰς ἑτέρους μεθίσταται τόπους τὰ πάντα πληρῶν. 2 Οὐ νόμων καὶ χρόνων ῥηταῖς τὸ θεῖον ὑπόκειται περιγραφαῖς. 3 Ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ σαφῶς ἴσασιν ἁλισκομένους ἐντεῦθεν ἑαυτοὺς, μεταβαλλόμενοι πλάττουσιν τὸ τῆς λήθης ὕδωρ, ὅ φασιν πίνοντας ἑκάστους τὰς τῶν οἰκείων βίων γεννήσεις ἀμνημονεῖν. Ὅτι δὲ ταῦτα μυθώδη καὶ πόρρω φιλοσοφίας ἐστὶν, οὐδεὶς τῶν εὖ φρονούντων ἔοικεν ἀγνοεῖν. Τί γάρ φαμεν, ὦ Πυθαγόραι καὶ Πλάτωνες· αὐτοὶ τὸ ληθοποιὸν ὕδωρ πεπώκατε λαβόντες;
thought_title: God fills all things; the water of forgetfulness is a myth
orientation: Eustathius opens his treatise by addressing Pythagorean and Platonist philosophers, first establishing that God is not confined by place, then attacking their myth of the water of forgetfulness.
pass_a_gloss: God fills all things, being limited by no one; for he who is not limited by place will be in every place entirely according to the Psalms of David; for if he should be said to be outside of some place, it is necessary that he be limited by that of which he is deprived; being whole therefore in all things, he in no way moves from one place to another, filling all things. The divine is not subject to fixed circumscriptions of laws and times. But since they know clearly that they are caught from this, changing themselves they fabricate the water of forgetfulness, which they say each one drinking forgets the births of their own lives. That these things are mythical and far from philosophy, no one of those thinking well seems to be ignorant. For what do we say, O Pythagoreans and Platonists: have you yourselves drunk the water of forgetfulness, taking it?

choices.why: Keeps the passive participle and the masculine singular 'no one' as the limiting agent, preserving the philosophical sense of a personal or quasi-personal limiter.

choices.english: according to the hymnody of David
choices.why: Renders the source's reference to David's psalmody literally as 'hymnody,' matching the brief's mention of David's hymnody.
Preserves the genitive relative with the passive of στερίσκω, keeping the logical force that the place of which God is deprived would limit him.
Keeps the adjective 'fixed' with the noun 'circumscriptions,' preserving the idea of definite, stated boundaries of laws and times.
Uses the glossary English for both λήθη and ὕδωρ, keeping the genitive construction.
Renders the compound adjective literally as 'forgetfulness-making' to preserve its force as a coined term describing the water's effect.

bible_refs.note: The statement that God is in every place and not limited by place echoes the Psalmist's declaration that there is no place where one can flee from God's presence.

pass_b_english: God fills all things and is limited by no one. For the one who is not limited by place will certainly be in every place, according to the hymnody of David. If he were said to be outside some place, he would necessarily be limited by that very place of which he is deprived. Being wholly present in all things, then, he does not move from one place to another, since he fills all things.
The divine is not subject to fixed circumscriptions of laws and times.

But since they clearly know that they are caught by this, they change course and fabricate the water of forgetfulness, which they say each person drinks and thereby forgets the births of their former lives. That these things are mythical and far from philosophy, no one of sound mind seems to be ignorant. For what do we say, Pythagoreans and Platonists? Have you yourselves taken and drunk the water of forgetfulness?
